value.overview: The Ruddy-capped Nightingale-Thrush (Catharus frantzii) is a small, mainly ground-foraging thrush of cool mountain forests in Mexico and Central America. It is recognized by its rusty-red crown, olive-brown upperparts, grayish face and breast, pale belly, dark upper bill, and orange lower mandible. The species is generally shy and solitary, spending much of its time in dense understory vegetation. Costa Rica supports a resident population in its major highland ranges.
value.classification: The species belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, and the genus Catharus, which includes several Neotropical nightingale-thrushes. It was described by Jean Cabanis in 1861 and is sometimes called Frantzius's Nightingale-Thrush.
value.identification: This medium-small thrush has olive-brown to russet upperparts, a distinctly rusty or reddish-brown crown and nape, and a grayish face. The throat and breast are dull gray or olive-gray, becoming paler toward the whitish belly. The bill is dark on the upper mandible and orange-yellow on the lower mandible; the legs are pale pinkish to brownish. Sexes are similar. It is often detected by its clear, flute-like song from dense montane vegetation.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy-capped Nightingale-Thrush ranges from Mexico south through Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a relatively common resident of the mountains, occurring on both slopes and in the northern cordilleras generally above about 1,350 meters, and commonly from roughly 1,500 to 2,500 meters in the Central Volcanic and Talamanca ranges. It favors humid montane evergreen and cloud forests, especially dense understory, but also uses bamboo thickets, forest edges, tall second growth, and other well-vegetated clearings.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration. Some populations may make limited local or partial movements along elevational gradients, but Costa Rican birds are generally considered sedentary.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica is reported mainly from April through June, although singing and nesting activity can extend into July in some areas. The female builds a bulky cup nest of moss, liverworts, rootlets, grass, vine pieces, and other plant fibers, usually 1–4 meters above the ground in a shrub or tangled understory. Clutches commonly contain two pale grayish or blue-green eggs marked with cinnamon or brown spots. Dense, well-concealed vegetation is important for nesting success.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, supplemented with berries and other soft fruit. It usually searches on the ground or in low vegetation, moving through leaf litter, moss, roots, and dense understory. It normally forages alone, although pairs may feed in the same area during the breeding season. Occasional observations include following army-ant swarms and taking small vertebrate prey such as frogs.
value.behavior: Ruddy-capped Nightingale-Thrushes are secretive, generally quiet when not singing, and usually remain within dense forest understory. They hop or make short movements along the ground while searching for prey and may perch quietly on low branches. Individuals are commonly solitary, while pairs are more likely during breeding. Males defend territories with clear, repeated songs, especially during the breeding season. The species is more easily heard than seen in thick cloud forest.

conservation.populationTrend: No clear global population decline has been established, although regional populations may vary with habitat condition.
